identification.name: Nitinol (NiTi Superelastic Alloy)
identification.common_form_notes: Most commonly supplied as fine wire, which isn't well represented by this database's form options — treat Round Bar/Tube as the closest available approximations. Conventional machining is difficult: Nitinol work-hardens rapidly and its superelastic springback resists clean cutting, so wire forming, laser cutting, grinding, and EDM are far more common than milling/turning.
identification.notes: A "smart material" comparison/inspiration entry, not something a capstone team would typically source and machine themselves. This is the superelastic grade (as opposed to the separate shape-memory-effect grade also in this database): its austenite finish temperature (Af) is set below the intended use temperature, so it's already austenitic at room/body temperature and needs no heating to work — applying stress mechanically induces a reversible martensite transformation, giving large recoverable strain without a permanent temperature change. Tensile Set (0.10% permanent set after 6% imposed strain) is the standout figure here: roughly 98% of a 6% strain fully recovers on unloading, versus ~0.2% recoverable strain for a conventional structural metal — this is the single number that best captures why superelastic Nitinol is used at all. "Tensile Strength, Yield" (814 MPa) is labeled by the source as the stress "of martensite after transition" — i.e. the stress-induced-martensite plateau stress where the pseudoelastic strain plateau occurs, not a conventional 0.2%-offset yield in the dislocation-slip sense; recorded here as the yield strength value, the closest available property, but the underlying mechanism is different from every other yield strength value in this database. Elongation at break (17.5%, stored as ductility) is distinct from the source's separately-reported "max strain recovery" of 8% (the recoverable superelastic strain) — both are real but represent different concepts (total ductility to fracture vs. how much can be recovered elastically). IMPORTANT DATA GAP: this source doesn't report the Af transformation temperature or elastic modulus; a supplementary Goodfellow technical overview gave only general alloy-family ranges (not specific to this grade): Young's modulus ~20–50 GPa martensite / ~40–90 GPa austenite, and superelastic grades intended for room-temperature use typically target Af around 0–20°C (just below body/room temperature) — general web sources report an "upper plateau stress" of roughly 500 MPa for medical-grade superelastic wire, in the same range as this datasheet's 814 MPa figure but not a direct match, so not stored as a property value. Nitinol is generally weakly paramagnetic (not ferromagnetic) — practically important since it makes superelastic medical devices MRI (magnetic resonance imaging)-compatible. Shear strength is not derived via von Mises for the same reason as the shape-memory grade: transformation-based deformation doesn't behave like conventional ductile yielding.

typical_usage: Flexible/compliant mechanisms needing large recoverable deflection without permanent set: orthodontic archwires, eyeglass frames, medical stents and guidewires, and superelastic springs/connectors. Chosen over a conventional spring metal when the application needs far more recoverable strain (6-8% vs. ~0.2-0.5%) than ordinary elastic deformation allows, at a fixed operating temperature (no heating step required, unlike the shape-memory grade).
